PLOS Biology.title: The importance of genes does not predict their mutation rate
PLOS Biology.abstract: by Sofia Radrizzani, Laurence D. Hurst The convention that mutation is a random process has been challenged by suggestions that selection has acted on between-gene variation in the mutation rate, with claims that more important genes are protected from mutation in part, in prokaryotes, by being on the leading strand, while those required for rapid adaptive evolution have higher mutation rates, in part by being on the lagging strand. The original selectionist claims have proven contentious with several replication failures. However, none of the replication attempts fully allow for covariates and many employ data from mismatch repair (MMR) knockout strains. To address these limitations, we consider amassed mutation accumulation data for wild-type Escherichia coli, the focal species for adaptive claims, and Saccharomyces cerevisiae, in a multiple parameter-controlled analysis to predict between-gene variation in mutational density (mutations per base pair). Along with covariates, we consider putative selectively relevant parameters: protein level and essentiality to capture genic “importance”, and, in E. coli, strand with respect to DNA replication. We consider deviation of correlation and partial correlation values from those expected under trinucleotide-controlled simulations. While in E. coli more highly transcribed genes may have slightly lower mutation rates, potentially consistent with a selectionist model, the same is not seen in yeast, and in neither species do genes for more abundant or essential proteins have lower mutation rates. In E. coli there is no difference in mutation rate between genes on different strands, a lack of difference replicated in other prokaryotes. The degree of purifying selection is also not predictive of mutation density. We additionally highlight a strong artefact seen using the standard off-the-shelf statistical approach and note that results from MMR-deficient strains are discordant. We conclude that as trends are nearly uniformly unsupportive, not consistent between species and of miniscule effect size, they present no challenge to convention.

PLOS Biology.title: Neural integration of acoustic statistics enables mice to detect acoustic targets in noise
PLOS Biology.abstract: by Artoghrul Alishbayli, Karol Przewrocki, Paul van Heumen, Bernhard Englitz Sound detection amidst noise presents an important challenge in audition. Many naturally occurring sounds (rain, wind) can be described and predicted only statistically, so-called sound textures. Previous research has demonstrated the human ability to leverage this statistical predictability for sound recognition, but the neural mechanisms remain elusive. We trained mice to detect vocalizations embedded in sound textures with different statistical predictability, while recording and optogenetically modulating the neural activity in the auditory cortex. Mice showed improved performance and neural encoding if they could sample the statistics longer per trial. Textures with more exploitable structure, specifically higher cross-frequency correlations improved behavioral performance as well as neural representation of vocalizations. Activating parvalbumin-positive (PV) interneurons had an asymmetric effect depending on the acoustic context, improving detection and neural encoding of vocalizations for low correlations, and impoverishing them for high cross-frequency correlations. In summary, mice exploit stimulus statistics to improve sound detection in naturalistic background noise, reflected in behavioral performance and neural activity, relying on PV interneurons for temporal integration.

PLOS Biology.title: Category learning drives cortical attentional gain to diagnostic dimensions of perceptual information
PLOS Biology.abstract: by Sahil Luthra, Raha N. Razin, Adam T. Tierney, Lori L. Holt, Frederic Dick Humans and other animals develop remarkable perceptual and cognitive specializations for identifying, differentiating, and acting on classes of ecologically important signals. This expertise is flexible enough to support diverse perceptual judgments: a voice, for example, simultaneously conveys what a talker says, as well as myriad cues about her identity and state. Expert perception across complex signals thus involves discovering and learning regularities that best inform diverse perceptual judgments, as well as weighting this information flexibly as task demands change. Here, we test whether this process may involve attentional gain. We use two prospective auditory category learning tasks to relate a complex, entirely novel soundscape to four classes of ‘alien identity’ and two classes of ‘alien size.’ Identity, but not size, categorization requires discovery and learning of patterned acoustic input situated in one of two simultaneous, non-overlapping frequency bands. This allows us to capitalize on the coarsely segregated, frequency-band-specific channels tiling auditory cortex. We use fMRI to ask whether category-relevant perceptual information present in one frequency band is prioritized relative to simultaneous, uninformative information in the other frequency band. Only among participants expert at alien identity categorization do we observe neural prioritization of the identity-diagnostic frequency band. This prioritization persists even when the diagnostic information becomes irrelevant in the size categorization task. Tellingly, the neural selectivity evoked implicitly in the identity categorization task aligns with that in an independent task, where activation is driven by explicit and sustained selective attention to pure tones in one or the other frequency band. Additionally, the learning trajectories taken to achieve expert-level categorization leave fingerprints on the patterns of neural activity associated with the diagnostic dimension. In all, this indicates that learning categories can drive attentional gain to category-diagnostic input dimensions.

PLOS Biology.title: Life-cycle plasticity enables conditional asexual reproduction in a kelp
PLOS Biology.abstract: by Daniel Liesner, Rémy Luthringer, Lineekela Kandjengo, John J. Bolton, Mark D. Rothman, Myriam Valero, Fabian B. Haas, Susana M. Coelho Many organisms alternate between distinct life stages and can reproduce either sexually or asexually, yet the mechanisms coordinating these developmental and reproductive transitions remain poorly understood. Here, we investigate the molecular basis of life stage identity and reproductive mode in the kelp Laminaria pallida, a multicellular organism with a complex life cycle. By combining gene expression analyses with developmental experiments and natural population-level approaches, we characterize the transcriptional signatures associated with developmental state transitions in both sexual and asexual contexts. We show that asexual reproduction is associated with endoreduplication and reduced fitness, while it is retained but rarely expressed in two natural populations. Moreover, we find that the presence of potential mating partners reduces asexual development, revealing that reproductive mode is adjusted in response to reproductive opportunities. Together, these findings suggest that asexual reproduction functions as a conditional alternative to sex, promoting persistence when sexual reproduction is constrained while preserving the long-term benefits of sexual reproduction when mates are available. More broadly, our results reveal how organisms integrate developmental, environmental, and reproductive cues to balance alternative reproductive strategies across complex life cycles.

Briefings in Bioinformatics.title: Explainability in transformer-based models: methods, tools, and applications in natural language processing and bioinformatics
Briefings in Bioinformatics.abstract: AbstractIn recent years, Transformer-based models have become state of the art in natural language processing (NLP) and have achieved exceptional performance in a wide range of tasks. Their impact has extended to critical domains such as healthcare and bioinformatics. Transformer models are nonlinear and complex, making it challenging for researchers to understand different aspects of model performance and decision-making processes. Given the widespread use of these models in data processing, particularly in applications related to human health, the need for interpretable and transparent models has become essential. The goal of this paper is to provide a comprehensive review of explainability methods for transformer models, as well as the interpretability tools commonly used in NLP and bioinformatics. First, interpretable methods in different domains are broadly categorized. It then presents a focused discussion on strategies for explaining transformer-based models. By analyzing and comparing these methods, their strengths, applicability to transformers, and limitations are highlighted. As model complexity increases, understanding model behavior becomes more challenging. Explainability techniques can help address this gap and support tasks such as error diagnostics, model improvement, and other applications. Greater clarity in a model’s decision-making process can increase user confidence. Interpretable models are particularly important in critical applications such as drug design, where they can support deeper investigation and facilitate new discoveries. Finally, this paper outlines potential directions for future research.

Briefings in Bioinformatics.title: CRAFT: an antigen-specific TCR generative model for conditional de novo design with physicochemical constraints
Briefings in Bioinformatics.abstract: AbstractT-cell receptors (TCRs) are essential to adaptive immunity and mediate the recognition and elimination of malignant or infected cells through antigen-specific interactions. Despite the clinical progress of TCR-based immunotherapies, computational de novo design of antigen-specific TCRs remains difficult. The main difficulties include the complexity of peptide–major histocompatibility complex (pMHC)-dependent recognition, strict physicochemical requirements at the binding interface, and the small amount of paired training data available for model development. Current generative approaches depend largely on 1D sequence statistics and do not capture pMHC presentation context, interfacial physicochemical properties, and native receptor priors within a unified framework. We present conditional reconstruction of antigen fragments for TCRs (CRAFT), a decoupled generative model for pMHC-conditioned de novo design of antigen-specific TCR CDR3$\beta $ sequences under physicochemical constraints. With large-scale pretraining, CRAFT learns base representations that help reduce the limitations imposed by data scarcity. We further incorporate antigen-derived contextual information to guide antigen-specific TCR CDR3$\beta $ sequence design. The architecture comprises an antigen encoder (PrimeBERT) that captures the pMHC context and an autoregressive decoder (PrimeTCR) that preserves native receptor priors. The encoder and decoder are coupled through cross-attention and augmented with Atchley factor embeddings, allowing CRAFT to incorporate physicochemical constraints relevant to antigen-conditioned receptor design during sequence decoding. Across multiple evaluations, CRAFT demonstrates competitive sequence naturalness, together with favorable performance in specific binding, and predicted structural plausibility. Overall, CRAFT provides a computational framework for developing personalized tumor immunotherapies. It also holds potential to support clinical translation by enabling the efficient, targeted discovery of candidate TCRs.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: SnoDB 3.0: a specialized database featuring murine and human annotation and cross-species correspondence for the snoRNA community.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: Small nucleolar RNAs (snoRNAs) are a large, evolutionarily conserved family of non-coding RNAs that guide ribosomal RNA (rRNA) modifications. Recent years have seen growing interest in the biological and biomedical roles of snoRNAs, their guided rRNA modifications, and their alternative functions. snoDB is a specialized database that aggregates human snoRNA annotations and features, including genomic location, host gene, conserved motifs, protein and RNA interactors, expression levels, as well as rRNA target sites and modification levels. In this third release, we expand the database to include murine snoRNAs with an equivalent level of annotation, update human snoRNA host genes, RNA interactors and protein interactors, and introduce new tools to establish snoRNA and rRNA target cross-species correspondence. snoDB 3.0 is available at https://bioinfo-scottgroup.med.usherbrooke.ca/snoDB/.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: PANTHER: the protein tree and function resource in 2027.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: PANTHER (Protein ANalysis THrough Evolutionary Relationships) is a comprehensive resource of phylogenetic trees of protein-coding gene families. Trees are manually annotated with Gene Ontology (GO) terms describing how protein functional characteristics were gained and lost over time along tree branches, and these evolutionary models are used to create GO annotations for protein-coding genes. Orthologs, paralogs, and xenologs are assigned based on the trees. Here, we describe updates to the PANTHER resource since our previous published report in 2022. Since that time, the content of the database has been systematically improved: GO annotations of the trees have been expanded to increase coverage of genes by 20%-100% depending on the organism; thousands of families have been revised and ~100 added; and the PANTHER release pipeline has been modified to improve stability of the trees across versions. The expanded annotations for all 131 genomes in the PANTHER trees can be downloaded or used for analyzing gene lists directly on the PANTHER website, and users can now generate tree-based GO annotations for any sequence file using InterProScan.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: KinaseMD 2.0: an updated database of kinase mutations and drug response.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: Kinase mutations can alter activity, inhibitor response and downstream phosphorylation signaling, particularly within four resistance-associated substructures: gatekeeper, G-loop, αC-helix, and A-loop. KinaseMD 2.0 (http://modinfor.com/KinaseMD/) updates the kinase-centered database in three areas. Integrating source-curated annotations with Dr. Kinase predictions expanded substructure annotations from 1162 to 13 522 and kinase coverage from 388 to 547. Updated pharmacogenomic and signaling layers contain 422 244 drug-response measurements, 1614 candidate drug-resistance evidence records, and 359 600 predicted phosphorylation-network rewiring events. The new Kinase Perturbation Evidence Mapping (KPEM) workflow combines LLM-based literature extraction from an initial collection of over 480 000 publications with standardized processing of 30 public drug-treatment phosphoproteomic datasets. It provides 23 757 kinase-level records of literature-reported evidence and 53 029 phosphoproteomic records across 5124 drug/agent categories and 1598 disease contexts, distinguishing reported phosphorylation evidence from inferred kinase-associated signaling responses. By linking resistance-associated substructures, cancer mutations, drug response, and phosphorylation signaling, KinaseMD 2.0 supports studies of drug-resistance mechanisms and kinase-inhibitor design and development.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: CATH and TED in 2026: expansion in the number and diversity of CATH superfamilies.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: CATH (https://www.cathdb.info) is a widely used bioinformatics resource that classifies protein structural domains from the wwPDB and integrates evolutionary, structural, and functional annotation alongside interactive visualization and analysis tools. CATH is recognized as a Core Data Resource by ELIXIR and a Global Core Biodata Resource by the Global Biodata Coalition. CATH continues to expand its coverage of protein structure space by integrating experimentally determined structures from the Protein Data Bank with the rapidly growing collections of predicted structures from the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database as part of The Encyclopedia of Domains, the new sister resource of CATH. We provide an update on advances in new homology detection protocols and automated workflows providing end-to-end domain annotation and classification for processing large-scale protein structural data.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: The Chemical Probes Portal-2026: expanding and enhancing this expert review-based public resource to sustain chemical probe selection and application in bioscience.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: The Chemical Probes Portal (https://www.chemicalprobes.org) is an open, international, resource empowering scientific robustness by supporting responsible research using chemical probes. The Portal informs best-practice in the selection and application of small-molecule chemical probes through expert review, manual curation, and community engagement. Used correctly, high-quality chemical probes are powerful, versatile research tools enabling the fundamental study of protein function, target validation, and development of new therapeutics. Conversely, the inappropriate selection and use of these chemical tools can compromise experimental interpretation, reliability, and translational impact, highlighting the need for trusted advisory resources. The Portal addresses this challenge, providing a unique collection of curated data, expert reviews, and related guidance. We describe significant developments to the Portal's content and infrastructure. We have substantially expanded the content, with curated probes increasing by 26% since our last update. We have significantly enhanced website functionality through implementation of new, more informative probe pages, improved search tools and enhancements in data accessibility, machine readability, and interoperability. Together, these developments strengthen the Portal as a trustworthy, user-friendly provider of expert-reviewed chemical probe information and an increasingly valuable source of gold-standard FAIR, accessible data in the era of AI-assisted information discovery, underpinning reliable bioscience research.

eLife.title: Cis-regulation and natural selection in the evolution of human DNA methylation
eLife.abstract: The vast collection of human-specific traits—such as our unique morphology, cognition, behavior, and diseases—has long been attributed to gene expression divergence between us and our closest living relatives, chimpanzees. Theory suggests that changes to cis-regulatory elements such as promoters and enhancers may drive evolutionary adaptation, and DNA methylation is a key factor in transcriptional cis-regulation. However, we still lack an understanding of (1) how species-specific methylation patterns arise; (2) their downstream effects; and (3) whether they are a common target of natural selection. In this study, we investigated these three questions. By combining a novel hypothesis testing framework with DNA methylation data from six human and chimpanzee cell types, as well as fused interspecies hybrid cells, we disentangled cis- vs. trans-acting methylation divergence across the genome. Across cell types, we found that methylation divergence is primarily driven in cis, which can be linked in some cases to nearby sequence variants such as CpG gains and losses. Although less common, regions with trans-acting methylation divergence were enriched for specific transcription factor (TF) binding motifs, suggesting a role of TFs such as FOXM1 in these differences. Having established these causes of methylation divergence, we then examined the functional consequences of differential methylation. Although methylation lacks a consistent relationship with transcription, we observed that associations between methylation and gene expression are stronger for genes with cis-regulatory divergence. Moreover, we identified lineage-specific selection shaping promoter methylation at the level of entire pathways, including those associated with human-specific traits such as speech, cognition, and susceptibility to infection with hepatitis C. Collectively, our findings provide a mechanistic framework suggesting that DNA methylation may occupy a key position, mediating the effects of both cis- and trans-acting factors on transcriptional networks, including those contributing to human-specific traits.

eLife.title: Learning-associated flexibility of cortical taste coding is impaired in Shank3 knockout mice
eLife.abstract: The ability to update the valence of sensory perception to influence behavior is crucial for survival. A common phenotype in autism spectrum disorders (ASDs) is defects in sensory processing, but whether these defects impair flexible sensory encoding is largely unexplored. In particular, how genetic risk factors such as Shank3 deletion affect the adaptability of cortical taste processing and downstream behavior is unknown. To address this gap, we performed two-photon calcium imaging during a conditioned taste aversion (CTA) learning paradigm, an ethologically relevant form of associative learning that depends on taste processing in the gustatory cortex (GC), to examine how Shank3 knockout alters taste-related neuronal activity in GC and influences CTA learning. We found that GC neurons in Shank3 knockout mice exhibited reduced stimulus-evoked suppression and increased trial-to-trial correlated variability during the acquisition of CTA memory. These activity changes, which likely reduced signal-to-noise ratio in GC, were associated with slower CTA acquisition in Shank3 knockout mice. In both genotypes, CTA learning enhanced, while subsequent extinction reduced, taste discriminability in GC, and both extinction and the associated reduction in discriminability were faster in Shank3 knockout than in wild-type mice. Together, these results show that Shank3 loss is associated with destabilized cortical activity dynamics in GC, which may contribute to inefficient encoding and maintenance of learned taste aversion. These findings show that loss of Shank3 compromises the ability of animals to update behavior to incorporate negative outcomes, and suggest this loss of flexibility may be an important feature of monogenic ASDs.

eLife.title: Synthetic torpor in the rat protects the heart from ischaemia-reperfusion injury
eLife.abstract: During times of environmental stress, many animals enter torpor: a reversible protective physiological state typically characterised by reductions in core temperature, heart rate, and oxygen consumption. Species that naturally enter this hypothermic and hypometabolic state are tolerant of ischaemia-reperfusion injury. Consequently, there is a growing interest in utilising aspects of torpor for clinical applications such as protection from stroke or myocardial infarction. It is currently unknown, however, whether a torpor-like state is protective in animals that do not naturally enter torpor. Using viral vector-mediated chemogenetic activation of the medial preoptic area of the hypothalamus, we induced synthetic torpor in the rat, a species that does not naturally enter torpor. We demonstrate this state is cardioprotective in an ex vivo ischaemia-reperfusion injury model with an ~40% reduction in infarct size. Synthetic torpor-induced cardioprotection of the normothermic, isolated heart is not dependent on prior hypothermia in vivo. authors: Manolo F. Perez, Anna Zhukova, Renny Doig, Olivier Gascuel, Caroline Colijn
Trends in Microbiology.abstract: We are currently witnessing an unprecedented rise in the amount of diverse data on pathogens and epidemics. These data include genomic sequences with metadata such as geographic locations, risk groups, and sampling information. Machine learning (ML) has been applied to overcome the scalability bottlenecks inherent in these heterogeneous and high-dimensional datasets. This review highlights how ML tools are achieving concrete successes in predicting pathogen adaptation and drug resistance, performing source and host prediction, identifying high-risk lineages, and estimating phylodynamic and epidemiological parameters. We also show how ML is transitioning molecular epidemiology from a retrospective monitoring field to a proactive and predictive framework for major global microbial threats. Finally, we discuss the limitations of these approaches with respect to interpretability, uncertainty estimation, data volume requirements, and model misspecification.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Spatiotemporal recurrence and dissemination of Salmonella subpopulations in surface waters of central Chile.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: Agricultural waters have been identified as one of the primary sources of Salmonella contamination, which has resulted in numerous outbreaks associated with the consumption of contaminated produce. Consequently, an improved understanding of Salmonella contamination of agricultural waters could facilitate the development of control strategies to prevent food contamination. The objective of this study was to examine the diversity and spatiotemporal recurrence of Salmonella isolates in surface water related to agricultural activities. Water samples (n = 2,690) were collected between 2019 and 2024 in central Chile using modified Moore swabs, and whole-genome sequencing was carried out for 1 to 10 Salmonella isolates per sample. Non-clonal genomes from each sample (n = 1,034) were analyzed, showing that the most frequently identified serovars were Infantis (14.6%), Typhimurium (10.8%), Newport (8.5%), and Enteritidis (5.8%). The highest antimicrobial resistance burden was shown by Salmonella Infantis, which carried up to 11 antimicrobial resistance genes simultaneously. Importantly, phylogenomic analyses revealed a highly clonal population structure among the most prevalent serovars and identified recurrent subpopulations that were repeatedly detected across multiple watersheds and consecutive years, including lineages associated with human infections. These findings provide genomic evidence that agricultural surface waters may serve as reservoirs and dissemination routes for recurrent Salmonella subpopulations in central Chile, including multidrug-resistant strains. Our work underscores the critical importance of continuous environmental surveillance and the integration of environmental and clinical genomic surveillance data to improve our understanding of the Salmonella ecology and inform evidence-based mitigation strategies aiming to protect public health.IMPORTANCESalmonella enterica is a leading cause of foodborne illness worldwide, and contaminated irrigation water is an important pathway by which this pathogen can reach fresh produce. By analyzing more than 1,000 Salmonella genomes collected from agricultural waters in central Chile over 5 years, we found that specific bacterial lineages persisted across multiple watersheds and years, including multidrug-resistant strains linked to human infections. These findings indicate that agricultural surface waters in Chile can serve as reservoirs and dissemination routes for recurrent Salmonella subpopulations. Our study highlights the value of continuous environmental surveillance and the need to integrate data from environmental and human sources to identify potential contamination sources and reduce the risk of foodborne disease.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Community science uncovers environmental azole resistance in Aspergillus fumigatus across Norway, including a novel tandem repeat variant (TR(62)).
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Azole-resistant Aspergillus fumigatus (ARAf) is an emerging global health concern, mainly driven by environmental selection caused by azole fungicide use. Despite reports of environmental resistance across Europe, data from northern regions remain scarce. Here, we conducted the first nationwide investigation of environmental ARAf in Norway using a community science-based air sampling approach. Volunteers across the country collected airborne fungal spores using passive sticky-seal traps during three sampling periods between 2022 and 2023. In total, 2,332 air samples from 398 locations were analyzed, yielding 1,583 A. fumigatus isolates. Azole resistance screening identified 15 resistant isolates (0.95%) from 14 locations across four out of five Norwegian regions. Minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) confirmed resistance to medical azoles and elevated MICs toward azole fungicides. Whole-genome sequencing revealed known environmentally associated resistance mechanisms, including TR34/L98H (n = 11) and TR46/Y121F/T289A (n = 2), as well as a TR46/Y121F/T289A/S363P/I364V/G448S variant (n = 1). In addition, a previously undescribed promoter tandem repeat variant (TR62) was identified in one isolate that exhibited multi-azole resistance. Population genomic analyses indicated that resistant isolates were genetically diverse and not restricted to a single clonal lineage, suggesting both local expansion and recombination within a structured population. Although the observed resistance frequency was low, the presence of globally disseminated resistance mechanisms in airborne spores across Norway demonstrates that environmental azole resistance is established in the region. This study provides baseline data on the frequency and distribution of environmental ARAf in Norway and contributes to international efforts to strengthen monitoring of antifungal resistance. [IMPORTANCE] Azole-resistant Aspergillus fumigatus (ARAf) is an emerging public health concern, yet data from northern Europe remain limited. This study provides the first nationwide investigation of the frequency, distribution, and genetic diversity of environmental ARAf in Norway. By combining community-based environmental sampling with whole-genome sequencing, we demonstrate that resistance-associated genotypes of international concern are established in the Norwegian environment and occur across multiple regions. These findings provide important baseline data for future surveillance and contribute to global efforts to monitor and understand the emergence and spread of antifungal resistance.

PLOS Computational Biology.title: Decomposition of the S. aureus pangenome reveals evolving genetic repertoire associated with adaptation and virulence
PLOS Computational Biology.abstract: by Siddharth M. Chauhan, Bernhard O. Palsson, Jonathan M. Monk Bacterial pangenomes are mosaics of vertically inherited chromosomal backgrounds and horizontally acquired mobile elements, yet existing analysis methods either assign each genome to a single phylogenetic group or treat genes independently, failing to resolve this composite architecture. Here, we show that non-negative matrix factorization decomposes the accessory pangenome of 1,398 curated Staphylococcus aureus genomes into 24 additive gene modules (“phylons”) that cleanly separate lineage-defining components from mobile genetic element repertoires, achieving 90% reconstruction accuracy with 96% precision. The additive representation, where each genome equals a primary lineage phylon plus one or more mobilome phylons, recovers known biology (clonal complex structure, immune evasion cluster types) and reveals previously uncharacterized structure, including multiple horizontal transfer events linking the CC30 and hybrid ST239 pandemic lineages. Annotation-independent validation with geNomad confirmed that 75–96% of mobilome phylon gene instances physically reside within prophage regions across all 1,398 genomes, while coordinate-level analysis of the remainder revealed prophage boundary effects, chromosomally integrated elements, and composite mobilome architecture rather than false assignments. External validation on 966 independent draft genome assemblies yielded zero false-positive lineage assignments (mean AUC = 0.996) with no dependence on assembly quality, and mobilome phylons discriminated human from livestock hosts and methicillin-resistant from methicillin-susceptible isolates without retraining. A lightweight projection tool, phylon_assign, enables rapid classification of new genomes. The generalization of this framework from Escherichia coli and Enterobacter to Staphylococcus aureus – species with fundamentally different pangenome structures – establishes non-negative matrix factorization as a scalable, organism-agnostic approach for resolving the modular architecture of bacterial pangenomes.
